items.title: AI data handling firm Ascend.io acquired by Apple
items.content_html:
Apple has acquired another AI firm, though this time Ascend.io is aimed at company data management rather than any consumer-facing product.

Apple has been continuously buying up AI firms, with the most recent ones being for specific features such as Huxe's automated podcast creation. This time, though, it has bought Ascend.io from Silicon Valley firm Ascension Labs in order to improve its own internal data management.

According to the EU's public listing of significant acquisitions, Apple closed the deal on June 30, 2026. Apple appears to have adopted new processes, though, as this purchase is again not specified as an acquisition.

Instead, as it was with Huxe and also audio editing firm Samplab, Apple is listed as having the right to "make employment offers to and hire certain employees" of the firm.

Apple also gets a "non-exclusive license to Ascend's intellectual property rights," as well as at least some of its patents. So in theory, other firms could yet license the same data tools.

In practice, it's presumably going to mean that the company's existing clients can continue using it. That client list is impressive, too, including:

  • News Corp
  • Marist
  • HarperCollins
  • Mattel

Just as with those two most recent acquisitions, Ascension Labs has posted a notice online about shutting down, but not mentioning either Apple or acquisitions. "Ascend is winding down operations as we prepare for our next great adventure," it says.

Unlike many Apple acquisitions, this one is not likely to become visible to users, the way that MotionVFX is becoming a huge addition to Final Cut Pro.

items.title: Size matters: South Korea spared iPad mini image's potentially offensive gesture
items.content_html:
Apple has chosen to use a different image in South Korea to promote the iPad mini in South Korea, likely over fears that the version used the rest of the world might resemble an offensive gesture mocking the size of someone's manhood.

The launch of the updated iPad mini with OLED has unexpectedly sparked a bit of controversy. One of its marketing images was edited due to allegedly displaying what could be considered an offensive gesture.

The regional online Apple Store for South Korea looks a lot like others around the world. However, according to ITHome, one image showing the thin profile of the iPad mini has had its hand removed from view.

The hand itself exists on other Apple regional websites, but is removed from view just in South Korea.

A mean-spirited gesture

The hand is palm-up, with the thumb and forefinger extended and gripping onto one end of the iPad mini from the right-hand side.

As it is, in most of the world this would be considered a fairly adequate way to show the iPad mini's thin size while still holding onto it. In South Korea, this gesture can be considered offensive to some observers.

In short, some take the hand gesture to be insulting the size of a man's manhood. For some online communities, it is used as a symbol for misandry.

It isn't a gesture that most people would take offense to, but it only needs a small and vocal audience to cause trouble.

The controversy over the so-called "C" gesture reached its height in 2023, reports the Korea Times, after a video produced for the Nexon game MapleStory included a similar gesture.

Online denizens thought it was used on purpose as a pro-feminist message.

As usual for the Internet, users started to try and find other instances of characters in Nexon's marketing imagery for other games to stoke the controversy.

The affair resulted in a public apology from the developers, as well as the promise of an investigation and the taking down of all related videos.

Cultural sensitivity

This is also not the only time Apple has avoided using the gesture on its website, specifically in South Korea. Imagery for the iPhone Air also lacks the fingers at the top of the regional page, while still appearing in other versions.

For a major multinational like Apple, it has to be mindful of cultural differences across multiple borders. What may be considered perfectly fine in one country may not be in another.

It's a challenge to keep up, but in this instance, Apple seems to have made the change preemptively rather than reactively, and without harming the meaning of the imagery either.

At least Apple worked the issue out beforehand. The last thing it needed was another penis-finger billboard situation on its hands.

items.title: Enormous iPhone Duo demand can be easily met, hints confident Foxconn
items.content_html:
Giving hope to people with long pre-order delays, manufacturer Foxconn appears to say that it can readily fulfill even the iPhone Duo's surge in demand.

It sold out the instant pre-orders opened, and then only a lucky few were able to buy the iPhone Duo in-store. But even as shipping times remain long, Bloomberg reports that Foxconn has been saying it can meet any firm's demand.

"We have over 240 sites in 24 countries all over the world," said Michael Chiang, CEO of Foxconn's parent company, Hon Hai, "which enable us to have a timely supply to our customers' demand whenever they need."

"So I'm quite confident that we can fulfill the demand," he continued.

No guarantees

Importantly, Chiang did not discuss the iPhone Duo or even Apple specifically. He was responding to the question with a broad description of Foxconn's capacity, rather than committing to a timescale for the iPhone Duo.

However, Chiang is reportedly key in the relationship between Foxconn and Apple. It was he who took Apple chief operating officer Sabih Khan on a tour of the iPhone Duo manufacturing line in October 2026.

That tour was of Foxconn's central China facilities. According to the new report, this "iPhone City" is where the iPhone Duo is primarily made.

It's not known whether any other sites or any other manufacturers are producing the iPhone Duo.

Apple has been moving much of its manufacturing away from China. However, the iPhone Duo is a complex new product, and typically it takes time before other companies get orders to make a first generation device.

items.title: iPhone Duo review: Proof that foldables don't have to suck
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo is far from perfect as a first-generation product, but it is a strong enough entry that will single-handedly lift foldables from passing fad to serious category for anyone.

Apple has a habit of entering a market much later than its competitors then defining it. While it's too early to say if that's the case with iPhone Duo, it is clear that sometimes different can be enough to break the mold.

Foldables first entered the market in 2019 as overpriced hunks of fragile plastic. While Android manufacturers have a better handle on build quality and feature sets in foldables seven years later, they still feel like incomplete experiments.

With that version of the foldable market on my mind, I was confused as to why Apple would bother with such a compromised device. The problem is, I was expecting Apple to release something like what already exists on the market.

Instead, Apple went its own way. It gave the iPhone Duo a sturdy hinge, that nano-texture inner display, and thoughtful design choices throughout.

iPhone Duo

The iPhone Duo is the first foldable iPhone, with a 50% larger display than the iPhone 18 Pro Max when opened.
Buy at AT&T
Buy at T-Mobile
Buy at Verizon

I was worried that a foldable would present the features of a smartphone and tablet in one and suck at being both. Again, that's the Android problem, with poorly thought-out app design and OS feature sets.

There have been hints to how Apple would approach a foldable in its product design for years. We didn't know to look for them, as they were hidden in plain sight.

Apple considered every aspect down to ensuring the aspect ratio was identical for the inner and outer display.

iPhone Duo review: Apple thought of every aspect a foldable could interact with iOS

The iPhone Duo isn't a poorly implemented iPhone posing as an iPad. It is an iPhone through and through, even down to the (mostly) excellent camera system.

Two or three days isn't enough to say anything meaningful or insightful about the device. So, here we are, a week after release, and almost two since our first time with the device.

iPhone Duo review: Displays

Apple's first iPhone with two displays doesn't hold back on either. They're both Super Retina XDR displays with identical aspect ratios so half the inner display is the same as the outer display.

They're always-on displays capable of StandBy mode thanks to 120Hz ProMotion adaptive refresh rates. They're color accurate, HDR, displays with 3,000 nit peak brightness.

Outer 5.4-inch display

I've seen some critical response to the outer display being only 5.4 inches. I get it, especially since I'm coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max.

iPhone Duo review: a small outer display

However, I'm only one fold away from a display twice the size. While I'm certain Apple will come out with a larger iPhone Duo in the future that I'll absolutely jump on, I'm quite happy with what's here now.

The outer display feels like a fun little pocketable device that works very well for iPhone use. After all, we've had smaller.

It's the classic glossy iPhone screen with a cutout for the selfie camera.

This is a new device and form factor, so I won't pretend that I've magically found my permanent workflow in a week. I feel like I'll be using this outer display most often.

There's something appealing about the squat display. I don't watch TikTok and never gravitated towards 16:9 vertical video formats, so this proportionality feels more natural for me.

Sorry, web and app developers. It's just another fixed proportion and size you're going to have to get used to. More on that in a while.

iPhone Duo review: Capturing photos on the outer display is a good experience

Apple's iPhone camera shoots at 4:3 by default, which looks great on the display. Contact Posters, StandBy widgets, and social media timelines all take advantage of the squat form factor in a way long and skinny displays don't.

The apps that haven't been updated for iPhone Duo look best on the outer display. They're just smaller versions of what you'd see on a standard slab iPhone, which is a fine in-between mode.

Open this thing up and you've got twice the real estate.

Inner 7.6-inch display

The first thing you'll notice is how optimized apps for iPhone Duo fill out the inner display. It's like having a larger canvas for the apps you love and not some blown-up version of the old one.

iPhone Duo review: an awkward Home Screen layout on the large inner display

Apple does need to do something about the Home Screen layout in portrait orientation. It's as weird and messy as the one on iPad mini.

The Nano Texture outer cover feels nice to the touch and hides the crease in the center well. Some angled lights will reveal that crease, but you'll never see it during normal use and viewing distances.

iPhone Duo is an orientation-agnostic device. There is no "correct" orientation for any given app, though some do look better one way over another.

Since the aspect ratio is identical for both displays the split view mode with two apps shows an app identically to how it looks on the outer display. Split view is really well thought-out on iPhone Duo and even gives you the ability to lock apps into a pair.

You can't have two apps stacked above each other in portrait mode, but there is a multitasking trick for that mode too. A video playing using Apple's system video player or from a compatible app like Netflix can be pinned to the top third in portrait mode.

iPhone Duo review: Apps like Apple TV take advantage of the various angles and orientations

The bottom portion of this mode is a unique size that developers have to target directly. Place the iPhone Duo into seated mode and it moves to a 50/50 view again.

Apple did something unique with iPhone Duo beyond simply having two displays. Having so many modes of operation and app pairings means no shape or form factor is wasted.

StandBy

I'm loving how smart StandBy mode is with iPhone Duo. You're getting the classic alarm-clock-style view in tent mode, while standing slightly open provides a side-by-side widget view.

iPhone Duo review: StandBy works great and no longer needs power

These systems are a combination of Apple Watch complications and iPhone widgets. I like that side-by-side view in standing mode since it can display a photo on one side.

When something is in Now Playing, it can take over one side of the standing StandBy view or the entire tent mode view. Either way, this is a fun way to display passive information with your iPhone.

I don't like using my iPhone during dinner or at restaurants, but I do tend to lay it on the table. However, now I can place it in a StandBy mode to have some cute photos on display, for example.

iPhone Duo review: Design

The iPhone Duo is the biggest departure from iPhone design in the history of the device. The squat outer display is so compelling, I find myself confused when I pick up the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

iPhone Duo review: A new design disrupting the aging platform

There is a not-small contingent that believes that slab phones have just become gigantic and awkward. They can stick out of your pockets, especially in smaller garments, and can feel top-heavy due to the camera system.

My iPhone Duo is barely thicker than my iPhone 17 Pro Max and slightly heavier. I know there have been complaints about the size and weight, but I find both totally ignorable after being used to the giant smartphone.

The closed iPhone Duo feels heavy and dense, but not in a way that's uncomfortable. Open it up and suddenly it is light and thin. Balanced in the hand.

Apple's polished titanium edges are color-matched to the glass on the back. I'm very happy with the blue iPhone Duo, though the color finish on the glass is highly susceptible to scratching.

Mike Wuerthele here at AppleInsider says that the in-hand adjustment process is not that all dissimilar to the iPhone 3GS or iPhone 4 form factor to iPhone 6 Plus. It's just finding a new pivot point for your hand, and we'll leave that to you to figure out on your own.

iPhone Duo review: The rear glass color scratches easily

Fingerprints collect on the metal surfaces, but the blue hides them unless you shine a light on them directly. The rear glass is slippery and MagSafe accessories leave a ring behind, though it can be wiped off.

The outer display is flush with the edge, so there's no protective lip. This is an interesting choice considering Smart Take requires placing the iPhone on this display.

Apple is clearly confident in its Ceramic Shield 2, though I'd have liked to have seen even a tiny lip to prop the glass up and away from flat surfaces. As a reminder, sand has some individual grains harder than Ceramic Shield 2 is. I guess that's what cases are for.

The inner display does have a lip around the edge. This prevents the display from rubbing against itself when closed, and that also means the audible "click" of closing the display is the edge smacking together, not the display cover.

iPhone Duo review: That's one thick camera bump

Apple's notorious camera bump returned and only covers a portion of the rear casing. It's a departure from the edge-to-edge camera plateau that has shipped in other recent iPhone models.

The outer display has a cutout for the selfie camera. It is visible as a black circle and the Dynamic Island animates out from this circle.

The inner display hides the FaceTime camera, though it is obvious in some lighting conditions. Since the camera needs an unobscured view, the Nano Texture isn't applied over the camera cutout.

You have to go looking for that under-display camera in most lighting, but at the right angle and the right light, it's visible. It's not really a problem during normal use.

iPhone Duo review: A tablet-like experience in your pocket

The Nano Texture does an excellent job at stopping reflections and harsh light from disrupting content. It is also great at hiding that crease, which can be felt when running your finger across it.

iOS 27.2 launched during my testing of the iPhone Duo, so I had a chance to use Apple Pencil with USB-C on it. It is a good Apple Pencil experience, though obviously is limited by what the USB-C model can do.

I don't feel like the inner display will wear down or easily break under extended Apple Pencil use, and this is borne out by the iPhone Duo using the same glass as the iPad. It feels responsive and normal on both displays.

Hinge

Apple did a great job of making sure the hinge is (mostly) an afterthought on iPhone Duo. It's the most important mechanism of the device, but it is so good you just open and close it without thinking.

iPhone Duo review: A large camera bump and hinge

I like that the hinge is strong enough to use in multiple angles besides open and closed. Viewing media like shows on Apple TV is great in the seated mode even if it feels a little small.

Apple also included a hinge angle API so apps know what mode and angle your device is being used in. Some games have even implemented hinge angles into the gameplay.

The iPhone Duo hinge is just another example of how Apple didn't go halfway with this product. While there is plenty to iron out, Apple provided a sturdy hinge and a well-thought-out ecosystem on day one.

Let's talk a bit about reports of that hinge breaking the screens, though. This is not happening at a large scale.

As of October 30, we've spoken to 20 Apple Stores, and they have all seen a total of six broken screens across them all. Furthermore, iPhone service "activations," meaning interactions with Apple Service for everything in total, aren't any higher than they were last year, or the year before, at this point across the board.

If this was a huge problem, those service activations would be notably higher, given that this is a new release where there wasn't one of this scale so close to the measured period in either 2025 or 2026. This obviously doesn't help you if you've got one, but the answer is the same.

And if you do get one, contact AppleCare. Document your issue, and you will get a service replacement either mailed to you, or handed to you at retail. Simple as that.

As a reminder, Watergate was the name of the hotel. Calling this "crackgate" or similar nonsense remains ridiculous.

Right now, we predict that if you're reading this in the distant future of 2027, those reports will just be a distant memory — but we are watching. If this changes, we'll let you know.

MagSafe

There were some rumors that suggested Apple wouldn't include MagSafe in the iPhone Duo. Those were clearly wrong, but there are some use case caveats.

iPhone Duo review: Original MagSafe wallets won't fit

You'll need a new MagSafe wallet for iPhone Duo, as the old ones just don't fit. Previous MagSafe wallets and battery packs were made for the longer iPhone design, so new ones need to be made squat. We've already seen a few pop out.

StandBy doesn't need to have power to work anymore, but MagSafe makes charging easy. And since tent mode makes the USB-C port point right, you can plug it in to charge in that mode too.

Your magnetic stand that holds the iPhone off the desk will work with the device closed, but not open. So, you'll need something new there too.

I expect accessory makers will have some interesting options for iPhone Duo in the near future. I'd love to see specific cases, wallets, and batteries acknowledge the various ways iPhone Duo can be used.

Touch ID

Apple wasn't able to get Face ID into the first generation iPhone Duo. This is upsetting to some, but as an iPad mini user, it was an easy transition.

iPhone Duo review: Touch ID returns since Face ID won't fit

Actually, Touch ID is quite easy to reach in most orientations so it isn't much of a thought beyond retraining that muscle memory and hold that I spoke about before. I will say, though, double pressing the button then resting to make a purchase is a bit more cumbersome than just looking at the device.

I'm glad that the Apple Watch can be used to unlock iPhone Duo. It's basically instant and no slower than using Face ID.

Touch ID has become something I only need to use when using Apple Pay or buying things from the App Store. Otherwise, I just swipe up and my iPhone unlocks right away.

This is not the same as using Apple Watch as a fallback option on other iPhones. That was a system made to use Apple Watch only when the user's face was obscured, like when wearing a mask.

It's just an evolution of the feature.

iPhone Duo Review: Dual Fusion camera system

I'll say this up front: this isn't the place to discuss iPhone Duo's cameras in detail. We are going to talk about it more, but it deserves a highlight of its own.

We've already started that, and that will be a deeper dive and compare later similar to one I did on iPhone 18 Pro's upgraded camera system. We're already several kilowords into that.

iPhone Duo review: Great cameras in a device full of trade offs

I will say this, now, though. Whatever iPhone you're coming from, other than iPhone 17 Pro or newer, this is an upgrade in some shape or form.

The iPhone Duo sensors are not identical spec-for-spec to the cameras used in iPhone 18 Pro. The sensor on the iPhone Duo is physically smaller, there is no variable aperture, you do not get ProRaw or ProRes, there is no LiDAR for rangefinding, and there is no optical telephoto camera which is the biggest and most obvious difference.

The slightly smaller main camera sensor size and use of hybrid focus pixels instead of 100% focus pixels means slightly less sharp photos in dim to dark environments, especially for moving targets. The larger sensor on other iPhone models will result in a sharper image, especially in shadowed areas of the image. Pixel peeping will be required to see the difference in most cases.

For nearly every iPhone Duo user, this distinction is almost meaningless. In normal circumstances, you'll never have a second different iPhone to compare near-identically framed shots, and as always the best camera is the one you have when you need to take the shot.

Instead, you'll have your photo you just took, and it'll look great. Yes, you can get a better photo by buying an iPhone 18 Pro Max, but that doesn't mean your iPhone Duo's photo is bad or even somehow unusable.

iPhone Duo review: Still capable of capturing amazing photos

I'm not going to waste your time going line by line down a specs compare page, this review is long as it is. The long and short of it is this — iPhone Duo will take near-identical photos to Apple's recent pro phones in most conditions other than low light.

Camera Control is here, but I did turn it into a dumb shutter button. All it does now is open the Camera app and take the photo. We've spoken about how to do this before, and we will do so again.

Okay, let's get into the cameras themselves.

48MP Fusion Main camera

Everyone seems desperate to assign some value to the iPhone Duo's Fusion Main camera. Everyone wants to know if it's an iPhone 17e under there, or even an iPhone 15.

iPhone Duo review: A competitive camera experience

Well, good news, it's better than that. Though the bad news is that I can't simply assign a value to it.

The iPhone Duo Fusion Main camera is a class of its own, for better and worse. There are elements of the iPhone 18 Pro camera system that make it better than even the iPhone 17 Pro Max, but the sensor size is comparable to the iPhone Air.

The two biggest differentiators for those upgrading will be the A20 Pro's image signal processor and the ability to manually set white balance compensation.

The A20 Pro provides access to Photographic Styles 3, which means texture and palette selection. There's also the new smart focus tracking that utilizes Apple Intelligence to keep locked onto a subject even if it exits the frame.

iPhone Duo review: Bright plus Film texture makes for good natural results

I think Apple's tuning for natural skin tone, contrast, and color profiles is its best yet. These decisions are baked into the camera's processing engine, which can be manipulated using Photographic Styles.

Texture control means you get to select whether to smooth skin, add some glow to highlights, or make things take on a film-like development style. Grain can be enabled for any of these, but it is an on or off toggle with no range control.

If you're coming from iPhone 17 Pro or anything else, these are big upgrades that give you more control over every shot. And since they're fully non-destructive, you can apply them or remove them at any time.

And like I said, iPhone Duo didn't get Pro Tools, but it did get the new white balance setting. It is something you can control with third-party apps on a more granular scale, but Apple's implementation is more than enough.

White balance is something you have to select per-shot and can't fix later, so keep that in mind. The auto setting is reliable enough that you can mostly ignore it, but those concerned with photography looks and a good eye should be able to tell when auto gets it wrong.

On all other iPhones beyond the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, white balance is an automatic system. But here, on iPhone Duo, I can note that it's tungsten or fluorescent lighting, daylight, cloudy, or shaded.

Doing so adjusts how warm or cold the entire image is and can make a photo look much closer to what the naked eye perceives. For example, iPhone 17 Pro Max wanted to show this leafy forest path as cold even though in real life it was warm and vibrant with fall colors.

The iPhone has a powerful computational photography pipeline, but it isn't always going to get everything right. I think it is somewhat funny that Apple chose to expose this setting on iPhone Duo, and thus providing a control over my photos not even available to the iPhone 17 Pro.

One other aspect of the iPhone Duo that I find interesting is its minimum focus distance. I can get much closer to a subject without automatically switching to macro mode.

Your food and pet photos are going to be much better on iPhone Duo than iPhone 17 Pro, funny enough. Yes, possibly even better than iPhone 18 Pro given it has a longer focus distance as well.

This aspect will undoubtedly go away in a future iPhone Duo that has a better camera system. However, it is nice that it is there today to provide one other small winning aspect over other camera systems.

iPhone Duo-specific camera features

Smart Take might just be my new favorite camera feature. I can easily set up and frame a group shot and have multiple usable options without having to fight timers or fiddly settings.

iPhone Duo review: Smart Take is an exclusive feature

Sure, you can just hand your iPhone to a stranger and ask them to take a photo, and Duo Preview is excellent for this. Although, being able to set all of the options and framing myself before automatically capturing images is the better experience.

Duo Preview will let whoever you're taking a picture of see what the image will look like. Though, that outer display doesn't show the entire frame, so keep that in mind.

Kid Cue is just a fun feature that I'll be taking advantage of. I like that it is Snoopy for now, but I hope third-parties can offer their own content for that later.

Finally, the iPhone Duo is an amazing selfie camera. Sure, the front-facing camera is fine, but you can now easily see yourself in the rear camera on the outer display.

I've heard others complain about the fiddly nature of some of these modes. I agree it can be very difficult to take a selfie this way the first time you try, but once you realize you can grip it and use the volume down button, you're set.

48MP Fusion Ultra Wide camera

I don't feel like I need to spend any time on the Fusion Ultra Wide camera. It is the same camera as the one found on iPhone 18 Pro and takes great photos.

iPhone Duo review: Macro shots are still possible with the Ultra Wide camera

Macro shots look great, but the closer focusing distance of iPhone Duo means you'll be using that mode less often. Ultra Wide cameras provide a unique, almost fisheye-like style that can be useful in some situations.

It's available for selfies too when using the outer display, but the quality of those shots at a close angle won't be flattering to anyone.

I'm glad the second lens is here even if I won't be using it as often.

Outer 12MP Center Stage camera

The outer display selfie camera is a more traditional experience with a lower spec. It is an older version of the camera that only offers a 12MP photo.

iPhone Duo review: The outer display has a cutout for the selfie camera

Here's all you need to know about the outer selfie camera — it exists. That's it. There's nothing remarkable here.

I'm glad I have a simple camera for video calls or use as a mirror in a pinch. It takes good-enough selfie pics, though on iPhone Duo, it's better to use the rear cameras.

I don't mind the cutout it creates in the display for the camera to exist. It also means the Dynamic Island is off to the side and out of the way of content.

Inner under-display FaceTime camera

The only notable aspect of the under-display FaceTime camera is that it enables Duo FaceTime. If you're on a call with someone, you can use the under-display selfie camera while showing another person with the outer camera.

iPhone Duo review: The inner display has an under-display FaceTime camera you can see if you squint

The inner and outer display will show the call participants so both users can see everyone. It really is an amazing experience and one everyone with an iPhone Duo should try.

Yes, the quality isn't great, and you're not going to use it for capturing selfies. That's fine, there are other cameras on this device for that purpose.

iPhone Duo review: Processor

Apple gave the iPhone Duo the same A20 Pro processor that is used in the iPhone 18 Pro. It has a 6-core CPU and a 7-core GPU with neural accelerators.

iPhone Duo review: Geekbench results show a powerful A20 Pro processor

There is a dual 16-core Neural Engine for even more powerful and prolonged on-device AI operations.

Apple says the battery life depends on which display you use, but mixed use results in something like 39 hours between charges. Of course, this is never what users actually encounter since they actually have third-party apps installed.

There are two batteries in iPhone Duo, which means two battery health indicators in Settings.

Games will drive that processor, heat up the case, and drain the processor like any other iPhone. That said, I can easily say the iPhone Duo battery life is at least on par with iPhone 17 Pro Max in my use.

iPhone Duo review: Emulation is great on iPhone Duo

I haven't noticed any issues with heat dissipation. When you're holding the iPhone Duo open, your right hand will rest around where heat will escape the device the most.

However, that slight increase in temperature is negligible and never uncomfortable. I think Apple's use of a vapor chamber helps keep things relatively cool.

This is the first iPhone I've had with a C-series Apple modem. My wife has had one in iPhone Air this past year without issue, and I have nothing notable to report about signal strength or performance versus previous models.

iPhone Duo review: A custom iOS experience

Just like with Apple Vision Pro, the strongest aspect of iPhone Duo is Apple's ability to blend hardware and software. That vertical integration can't be touched by any other smartphone company, and it isn't even close.

iPhone Duo review: Apple Vision Pro couldn't get the developer support it needed

Apple didn't just ship a foldable that runs weird iPhone apps on the outer display and iPad apps on the inner display. Instead, iOS was refactored into a custom design with special animations and design aspects for every portion of the device.

For example, I love how the wallpaper adapts to each view and angle on the Lock Screen. The opening and closing animation needs some polish, but that doesn't make it any less magical.

Sure, a new device shape means developers have to deal with the challenge of adopting their apps for each of the many ways a user can rotate or fold the iPhone Duo. Which of course also means that most apps won't be ready for the iPhone Duo at launch, or even now a week later.

iPhone Duo review: Adaptive Lock Screen wallpapers

This is a weakness today, right now, and it is less of one than it was when the embargoed reviews were published from pre-seeded iPhone Duo units that Apple gave out. In another week, it'll be less of a weakness. In a month, it won't matter.

Using non-optimized iPhone apps on the outer display is fine until the updates come through over the coming months.

I can say without a doubt that this isn't an Apple Vision Pro situation. The iPhone Duo is a certifiable hit in high demand and developers are already making money on projects tied directly to the device.

The apps will come.

iPhone Duo review: Games like 'No Man's Sky' needs to be updated

I can't wait until games like Minecraft and No Man's Sky are optimized for the dual displays. The emulator app Delta has already been optimized and is amazing for the platform.

I expect we're only just seeing the surface of what is possible when developing specific iPhone Duo features and games. While iPad mini has existed for some time, it never quite got the popular treatment and lacks the ability to fold.

iPhone Duo will show exactly what it's like to have a tablet in your pocket, and Apple's custom iOS interface enables that.

Living with iPhone Duo

I was highly skeptical Apple would ever enter the foldable category given Android manufacturers' failure to ignite interest in the category over 7 years. If Apple had shipped something similar to what Samsung or Huawei ships today, I would have been disappointed.

iPhone Duo review: Whimsy inside and out

Instead, iPhone Duo is somehow both great at being an iPhone while being something totally new. The outer display is gorgeous and feels fresh and fun to use.

The inner display literally opens up what is possible on iPhone. Apple Pencil integration is just the first of what could be many upgrades to the platform.

External display support is on my wishlist. If Apple did this, I wonder how I'd feel about my iPad Pro.

I have found that using the outer display is the easiest default for quick interactions. I check notifications, capture a photo, or log a meal from this display.

When I know I've got more than a single minute, I open the iPhone Duo up and use the larger inner display. I don't need to squint to read small text or notice the finer details of an image — it's all just there and looks great.

iPhone Duo review: Totally new yet familiar

I love that I can take a photo on my Sony a7II camera and sync the photos to my iPhone using an SD card reader. Then I can show the photos on the large inner display in all their high-resolution glory.

There are flaws, like the cutout being visible on the inner display in some light. The physical nature of the hinge frightens me a bit, as does the durability of the inner display.

I do have Apple Care One, so I don't have much to really worry about. However, I am very curious how this device will hold up over the weeks and months.

I'll definitely be babying the iPhone Duo more than other devices, at least for now. I don't like that the painted glass is so easy to scuff and scratch, so a magnetic leather back from Nomad is likely in my future.

I'll be reporting back at some point about living with the iPhone Duo for an extended period. This is my main iPhone and will be until at least September 2027, and honestly, I couldn't be happier with that choice.

iPhone Duo review - Pros

  • A unique iOS experience that makes both displays very useful for different reasons
  • Great cameras and features that won't make you miss that pro iPhone
  • Sturdy hinge, invisible crease, and excellent displays
  • A new "naked robotic core" that will undoubtedly challenge iPad's place in the future

iPhone Duo review - Cons

  • Easily scratched painted glass cover
  • Noticeably heavy when closed
  • No Face ID will be a problem without an Apple Watch
  • Visiting beaches will be a problem without a special case or sealed plastic bag

Rating 4.0 out of 5

Apple may have nailed the foldable form factor in one go, but I'm not going to pretend it's perfect.

This is a compromised device by nature. You're giving up a "pro" iPhone with maximum performance, cameras, and durability for something with a wider range of utility.

As apps and features are ironed out over the coming months, I'll have more to say about iPhone Duo as a product. I think what is most interesting about this product isn't what is available today, but what it means for the future of iPhone.

items.title: Russia orders Apple to surrender users' messages on demand
items.content_html:
Apple and Microsoft have been added to a Russian state surveillance registry, requiring them to hand over users' text, video and audio messages without a legal process, and by request.

Multiple firms and apps are already on this same list, including WhatsApp and Telegram, so it's not clear why it has taken until now for Apple to be added. It's a continuation of the country's moves to control users' messages, though, as it follows Russia's blocking of FaceTime in 2025.

According to Bloomberg, Apple and Microsoft were added to this registry of "organizers of information dissemination" on October 2, 2026. The registry is operated by the country's state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, which previously forced Apple to remove VPN apps from the App Store.

Now that Apple is on this registry, Russian law requires it to store local users' correspondence for up to three years. That data must be stored on servers within Russia, and it must be turned over to the country's security services as required.

Neither Apple nor Microsoft has yet commented publicly on the new requirements. Apple does observe the law in its international markets, but it has also removed features if it disagrees with those laws.

So when the UK ordered unwarranted access to user data in 2025, Apple disabled its Advanced Data Protection feature solely in that country. Plus it continues to not offer many features, and now also the HomeView, in the EU because of disputes over regulatory conditions.

Russia's demands on Apple and others

Back in 2022, Russian authorities fined Apple for not storing iCloud data on local servers. In that same year, Russia also made a legal requirement that major technology companies establish offices in the country.

Consequently, Apple opened an office in Moscow in February 2022.

Apple in Russia

Despite setting up that office, Apple has never had any Apple Stores in Russia. It also stopped online sales in the country in 2022 at the start of the attacks on Ukraine.

But Apple devices have been sold through third-party resellers for decades, and its services remained available to Russian subscribers until early 2026. That was at least in part because services such as the App Store are a grey area legally.

If a Russian iPhone user, for instance, subscribes to a Russian app, that in theory has nothing to do with Apple. But Apple runs the App Store and takes income from it.

So in March 2026, Apple reported itself to regulators. Since all non-US Apple sales are the responsibility of Apple Ireland, it was that division that reported the issue, and did so to UK regulators.

The UK ruled that Apple had breached sanctions against Russia "on the balance of probabilities." It fined Apple, and Apple ceased allowing such subscriptions to continue.

items.title: When to expect your pre-ordered Apple devices to ship
items.content_html:
Apple has launched a slew of new devices, and many of them start shipping on November 6. That date is going to be a good one to go check out an Apple Store, as depending on what you've pre-ordered, there may not be much reason to wait.

As ever, the devil is in the details of what precise configuration you've ordered. But, for instance, adding a nanotexture display to a MacBook Pro or an iPad will add delays.

iPhone Duo

There's actually some good news about iPhone Duo shipping dates, although don't get excited. Where up to very recently an order placed today would see delivery on January 25, 2027, it's currently showing as January 22.

After it's startlingly fast selling out, orders for the iPhone Duo are actually seeing some very small improvement in shipping times - image credit: Apple

That's for either color of the device, but also for the base configuration. All of the dates here are for the base models, except where certain features are only available with specific models.

Mac Studio

For instance, the latest Mac Studio has been out for some months and if you order many of the possible configurations today, they could be right in stock and ready to ship. That's the case with the M5 Max processor.

Apple is taking pre-orders for the 512GB Mac Studio, but you still have months to wait.

For the M5 Ultra edition, shipping is currently in 7 to 8 weeks' time.

Apple did finally announce a new configuration that is an M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB RAM. That's currently due to ship in 10-12 weeks, in January 2027.

MacBook Pro

If you ordered the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 processor when it was announced on October 27, you may have had cause to regret it on October 28 when the touch-screen tandem-OLED display version was launched.

That's especially because both the touch and non-touch 14-inch MacBook Pro are shipping on November 6.

This is still the case if you choose the nanotexture display option on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED. But it isn't if you go for nanotexture on the display of the 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED.

In that case, just selecting the nanotexture option pushes shipping back an entire day. Delivery will be on November 7 instead of November 6.

Things are a little more complicated with the non-touch 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple does still list most versions as shipping on November 6, but if you order silver with a nanotexture display, Apple is quoting 7-10 business days.

However, if you order the Space Black edition with nanotexture, things are very different. Placing such an order today gets you a quoted delivery date of between three and four weeks.

iMac

At least the iMac is easier. Pre-orders are open now and shipping will be on November 6.

The iMac is the one device you can still configure how you like and get it from the first day possible - image credit: Apple

For now at least, you can pick any configuration of color, storage, and RAM, and there will be no delay.

iPad mini

Back to the complexity and the delays we go. If you order the base 128GB iPad mini, you're fine, it'll arrive on November 6.

The new iPad mini sees delays if you want both a nanotexture display and cellular- image credit: Apple

That's the case whether you go for the Wi-FI-only or Wi-Fi plus Cellular model at 128GB. If you go for 256GB, though, you get the option of a nanotexture display and that can add delays.

Oddly, if you choose nanotexture glass, you still get it on November 6 unless you also specify that you want the cellular model. Then your delivery time is two to three weeks.

HomeView

The HomeView has perhaps been a little drowned out by all of the launches, but it's still had an impact. Originally due to ship on November 13, the table version of HomeView is mostly now back-ordered three to four weeks.

Most colors of the HomeView are now backordered - - image credit: Apple

There is an exception, though, as at time of writing the rose pink version of this model remains due to ship on November 13.

So does the wall-mounted HomeView, though, in either of its colors and all of its available mounting options. Apple is now saying that there's a Schneider Home Power Mount PoE Wired option coming, but it doesn't say when.

Buying in Apple Stores

If we've learned anything from the iPhone Duo's success, it is that it can still be worth going to an Apple Stores on the first day a device is due out. You'll definitely get to see and try one, for example.

It's more likely that you'll be able to buy any of these devices other than the iPhone Duo, too. But it is always the case that Apple Stores tend to stock the versions that will sell the fastest, which usually means the base model.

So if you want to buy a Mac Studio configured with 512GB RAM for an extra $15,500, you'll have to just order online and wait it out.

items.title: Up to 350,000 Macs exposed by a forgotten Popcorn Time updater
items.content_html:
An abandoned Popcorn Time updater left up to 350,000 Macs vulnerable to remote takeover, giving potential attackers a way to execute malicious code with full system privileges.

Security researchers at Eye Research detailed the discovery in an October 22, 2026, research report about Operation IXIM. The vulnerability affected Time4Popcorn, an abandoned fork of the popular BitTorrent streaming application that continued circulating under the Popcorn Time name after the original project shut down in 2014.

Some users had stopped using Popcorn Time, but its updater kept running. Eye Research discovered attackers could hijack it to install malware and intervened between November 2025 and March 2026.

How a forgotten updater exposed hundreds of thousands of Macs

The investigation began when Eye Research discovered an updater contacting an abandoned domain from a customer's Windows computer. Researchers registered the domain and found that approximately 50 requests were arriving every second from devices still running the software.

On macOS, the vulnerable component was a privileged helper called PT.updd, which launched automatically when the computer started. Like other macOS background services, the updater could run independently of the application itself, even when its owner wasn't actively using Popcorn Time.

The updater contacted its servers over unencrypted HTTP connections and accepted downloaded code without verifying its digital signature. On Macs, that code ran with root privileges, giving an attacker the ability to execute commands with the highest level of system access.

Anyone controlling one of the abandoned update domains, or capable of manipulating the network traffic, could potentially exploit the mechanism. The vulnerability was assigned CVE-2026-30612, although Eye Research didn't establish that criminals had already exploited it.

"We mapped a sample of the IP addresses using kepler.gl and they were everywhere." Image credit: Eye Research

Determining how many Macs were affected proved difficult. Researchers initially recorded approximately 1.7 million unique Mac identifiers, but later discovered that changes to a computer's hostname or network hardware addresses could cause the same machine to appear multiple times.

Eye Research revised its estimate to between 250,000 and 350,000 Macs. The company also estimated that approximately 2.5 million to 3 million Windows PCs had contacted the affected update infrastructure, although those figures aren't a verified count of individual devices.

Researchers used the vulnerability to disable the updater

With the original developers gone and no official patch available, Eye Research decided to use the vulnerable update mechanism to protect affected computers. The researchers developed a small update that disabled the background service responsible for checking for new software.

On Macs, the update ran a shell command that stopped the launch daemon responsible for starting PT.updd. The intervention didn't remove the application itself, and Eye Research said its repair was designed to leave other software and files untouched.

The approach raised legal and ethical questions because researchers were executing code on computers without their owners' explicit permission. Eye Research said it consulted its legal team and conducted extensive testing before deploying the update more widely.

The operation also encountered an unexpected obstacle involving antivirus software. On Windows, 11 security vendors initially detected the repair tool as malicious because it disabled an existing service, prompting researchers to modify their code to avoid those detections.

By December 2025, Eye Research reported deploying the update to more than a million systems. The campaign ultimately distributed more than 2 million update downloads, although that figure doesn't necessarily represent 2 million unique computers or confirmed successful repairs.

By March 1, 2026, the company was still delivering approximately 5,000 updates daily, representing a reported 98% decrease from earlier volumes. Eye Research subsequently ended the deployment and transferred 15 domains it controlled to the nonprofit Shadowserver Foundation in late March.

"A bit of debugging led us to this snippet of the code that was generating the hid." Image credit: Eye Research

The researchers couldn't obtain every domain associated with the abandoned software, leaving some update infrastructure outside their control. Their intervention substantially reduced the apparent exposure, but it doesn't guarantee that every vulnerable Mac received the repair.

Disabling the updater doesn't make Popcorn Time safe

Eye Research also discovered serious vulnerabilities in the main application that weren't addressed by the emergency update. The affected Time4Popcorn software uses a browser engine dating to 2014, with its security sandbox disabled.

The app loads JavaScript over unencrypted connections from domains its original developers no longer maintain. Researchers showed that malicious JavaScript could run programs on Windows, but they didn't demonstrate the same attack on macOS.

Disabling the vulnerable updater addressed only one security risk. The outdated Popcorn Time application could still expose users to malicious content and attacks that manipulate network traffic.

Abandoned software can remain a security risk long after developers stop supporting it. Even when nobody opens the application, privileged background processes can keep running without security updates.

How to remove Popcorn Time and protect your Mac

Mac users who installed the Time4Popcorn version of Popcorn Time should remove it, even if they haven't opened the app in years. Eye Research recommends a complete uninstall because disabling the updater doesn't fix the app's other security vulnerabilities.

Deleting apps from the Applications folder doesn't necessarily remove associated background services. Users can check for the vulnerable Mac updater by opening Finder, selecting Go > Go to Folder, and entering /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/ to look for a file named PT.updd.

The associated launch daemon is located at /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist. Eye Research's security advisory provides the specific Terminal command needed to disable the service if it's still present.

Mac owners should also keep macOS updated and maintain Apple's built-in malware protections. However, operating system security updates won't correct vulnerabilities in an abandoned third-party application.

The findings specifically concern the older Time4Popcorn fork and don't apply to a separate project that began using the Popcorn Time name in 2025.

items.title: It was the right time to add touch to the MacBook Pro, says John Ternus
items.content_html:
Apple has long resisted bringing touch support to the Mac, but it's finally made the jump with the new MacBook Pro. It's all because Apple felt it was the right time to make the change.

The MacBook line has been one of the most desired products to gain touch support for years. After countless rumors about it, Apple added the functionality to the PROLED versions.

However, making the change wasn't something that was done on a whim. According to a report from Wired, it needed the metaphorical planets to align first.

"The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard," insists CEO John Ternus, commenting on the years of insistence by Apple that it wasn't going to make a touch-enabled MacBook.

Even so, Ternus admits "I think there's times when it's comfortable and handy to have touch" on a notebook.

When it comes to actually making the change, Ternus claims Apple needed to "get to a point where adding touch didn't make the product lesser in any way." Apple didn't want a heavier or thicker device as a trade-off for touch support.

"That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we've ever put into a Mac," he continued. "All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well."

This is the first-ever touch-screen Mac - image credit: Apple.

To Greg Joswiak, touch was an overdue feature for some of its users, especially those in creative and engineering careers. They really wanted to work with the screen more directly.

"Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone," Joswiak said, meaning they're already naturally used to touch. "There's a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch."

Fixing wobble

Johny Srouji, chief of hardware, believes the quality of Apple's touchscreen is exceptional versus the rest of the market, because it does the hard work.

"If you're working on something easy, you're wasting your time," said Srouji. He wants the easy work outsourced, but for Apple to keep working on the harder tasks, like the display, touch support, and custom silicon.

That ethos has resulted in changes like a new thermal system to reduce the temperature of the display ready for a user's fingertips.

Srouji is also in the belief that the typical touchscreen notebook has a "wobble" when fingers touch the screen. A new hinge system was made to keep the display stable when it's touched by users.

When it comes to whether Apple is making a statement with its fall launch roster, the hardware lead insists it's business as usual for Apple. The company is still building the best products, and will ship them when it believes it's ready and complete.

items.title: Rian Johnson's Chromagraph Camera app brings his cinematic style to your iPhone photos
items.content_html:
Chromagraph Camera gives iPhone photos the Hollywood treatment for $12.99, but its cinematic look won't suit every photographer's taste.

Rian Johnson launched Chromagraph Camera, an iPhone photography app that uses image processing developed for his films. The "Knives Out" and "The Last Jedi" director worked with cinematographer Steve Yedlin and programmer Eric Cameron to bring Chromagraph Camera to the App Store.

So I recently badgered my cinematographer @steveyedlin into making my ideal iPhone still camera app. It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone's look processing and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies. https://t.co/makZzhFd2Q

— Rian Johnson (@rianjohnson) October 28, 2026

Chromagraph Camera captures RAW image data and bypasses Apple's standard photographic rendering in favor of the team's custom processing. Yedlin mentioned on Instagram that the app uses the same processing mathematics as his film work, but is adapted for Apple's cameras.

The approach gives photographs the team's preferred treatment of color, tone, grain, and halation. Users can also adjust color, tone, and texture, rather than relying entirely on the app's signature look.

If you're interested in trying it, you can snag it on the App Store for a one-time cost of $12.99.

It looks cinematic, for better or worse

I love camera apps. I'm hardly a photographer in any capacity, but I certainly take a lot of pictures.

Like a lot of hobbyists, my pictures have their own style to them. A lot of my friends and family have remarked that they can always tell my pictures from anyone else's.

Not entirely sure if that's intended to be a compliment, but I'll certainly take it as one.

Left: The Lettie G. Howard rigging (foreground) and Bicentennial Tower (background) | Right: Presque Isle State Park

My usual editing flow goes like this: I'll capture a picture on my iPhone 17 and then take it into VSCO to edit it. I used to use Halide, and one day I'll likely return to it; I really like bouncing around different apps.

That's why I bought Chromagraph as soon as Mike showed it to me.

Chromagraph is an interesting app, and as I said, I like trying out new stuff. As a bonus, Chromagraph is a one-time purchase of $12.99.

It's more or less point-and-shoot, which is nice. In fact, the first time you open the Chromagraph, it suggests that you replace your standard iPhone camera with it.

I won't be doing that, though, for one critical reason.

Chromagraph isn't a filter app, but it does give your pictures a very specific look. As the creators said, it replaces the iPhone's processing with the app's custom processing that is more in line with what its creators want.

The same subject taken with the default iPhone camera app vs Chromagraph, both images are unedited

And it definitely looks familiar. If you've watched any Blockbusters from the 2010s through now, you'll know what I'm talking about.

Film critic Katie Stebbins calls it "Intangible Sludge," and it's the hallmark of many a Hollywood film these days.

for an explicit example of how the Intangible Sludge has become standardized, look no further than a season 1 dexter screencap & a dexter: new blood screencap (pls do not @ me with "but he's not in miami anymore") https://t.co/3ubAZCI32Z

— Katie Stebbins (@_katiestebbins_) November 18, 2021

I should note that this is all personal preference, and I'm not saying that Chromograph isn't a good app. Chromograph just falls more on the David Yates end of the spectrum, while I fall more on the Wes Anderson end.

You can edit pictures you take within the app to compensate for the default look. I will say that it's nowhere near as intuitive as editing in many other photo apps, including Apple's own stock Photos app.

This addendum isn't meant to dissuade you from trying out Chromagraph, for the record. It's $13, and I've certainly spent more on less.

However, after I tried it, Mike asked me to include my opinion of it.

If you are looking for an app that gives you a ton of control, Halide is still our recommendation. You can get it for $19.99 per year, or pay $69.99 for a lifetime license.

items.title: It's back - the glowing Apple logo makes a return on MacBook Pro at last
items.content_html:
The first MacBook Pro that lacked Apple's iconic backlit logo was released in 2016. A decade later, it's back.

For a long time, the thing about the lit Apple logo on the lid of its portables was that it was the wrong way around. It was positioned for the user to see as they opened the lid, while it was then upside down for anyone passing by.

Never one to miss out on good advertising, Apple flipped that logo around. To this day its glowing symbol shines out from concert stages around the world.

It just also tells you how long it is since those concert musicians updated. Because the very first Apple laptop to eschew the lit logo was the 2015 12-inch MacBook, and then the first MacBook Pro was in 2016.

What it was

It was more symbolic than anything technical. Apple just cut out a hole in the shape of its logo and stuck some translucent plastic in there. Since the lid contained the backlighting for the front display, there was enough illumination to spare that this logo had a warmly welcoming glow.

But it was still an extra layer that room had to be found for. As the MacBook Pro got ever more thin and light, the thinness won and the light lost. Shortly after that first 2016 MacBook Pro lost its lit logo, they all did.

But it's back

Curiously, one of the features of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR models is that they are thinner. The screen, specifically, is significantly thinner enough to be called out by Apple as a selling point.

First look at the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and yes the Apple Logo on the lid lights up again! https://t.co/e5mEkGyXXx

— Rich DeMuro (@richontech) October 28, 2026

It's a feature of Apple using the tandem OLED display which dispenses with the usual backlight and extra layers of screen. Those layers made the screen clear, but they also meant more power was needed to make the display viewable.

And of course more layers meant more width. So by switching to tandem OLED, Apple has saved a quite remarkable amount of space. On the new 14-inch model, the screen is half a millimeter thinner, while on the 16-inch, it's almost a millimeter.

Despite achieving that thinness, Apple has chosen to reinstate the famous backlit logo. Perhaps it's again a function of the lit screen bleeding through, perhaps it was possible to do it without adding as thick a piece of translucent plastic and relying on the LED backlight as before.

But whatever the reason and however it was done, Apple has quietly called back to its distinctive past. It will now again be shining out from stages, and there will again be whole seas of lit Apple logos in classrooms and at events.

It wasn't the end of the world when the logo went, but if you were a longtime Mac user, you did feel it. So this is a good day.

And since the logo vanished under Tim Cook's watch, you have to wonder whether it's back because of John Ternus. He's not been CEO for very long, but he has been deeply embedded in the company's design teams for most of his time with the company.

items.title: Amazon's new Alexa devices are outfitted with Matter & Thread
items.content_html:
Apple's HomeView hasn't shipped yet, but Amazon is already staking out more of the smart home with five new Alexa devices designed for everything from entertainment to sleep.

The October 28 announcement follows Apple's recent expansion into smart-home displays. Apple introduced HomeView earlier in October, bringing Siri AI, facial recognition, and Apple Home controls to a shared household screen.

Amazon's latest products address some of the same needs, but the company is spreading those capabilities across several devices. Alongside its traditional speakers and displays, Amazon is introducing products designed specifically for the nightstand and displaying family photos.

Echo Show 16

The Echo Show 16 leads the announcements with a 16-inch full HD display, built-in Fire TV, and a 13-megapixel camera with night vision. Amazon has redesigned its interface with customizable layouts for family calendars, photos, and smart-home controls.

Echo Show with stand

The display also comes with an optional Nanomatte finish that Amazon says reduces glare by more than 90%. Customers can use the Echo Show 16 for video calls, streaming entertainment, or as a central dashboard for connected-home accessories.

Echo Dot

The new Echo Dot gets a more significant upgrade than its familiar spherical design might suggest. Amazon has added a built-in smart-home hub supporting Zigbee and Matter, along with a Thread border router.

Echo Dot

The Thread border router connects compatible Matter-over-Thread accessories to the home's IP network without requiring another Thread border router for a supported Alexa setup. Previous standard Echo Dot models could control certain Matter devices but didn't provide that Thread connectivity themselves.

Amazon has also added its AZ3 processor and a fourth microphone to improve voice recognition. The company claims the speaker produces 50% more bass than its predecessor, while a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender can expand coverage for customers with an existing eero network.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

The Echo Studio with Home Camera adds visual recognition to Amazon's premium speaker. Alexa+ can identify objects placed in front of the camera, answer questions about them, and let customers check on a room remotely through the Alexa app.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

Amazon plans to add video calling through compatible Fire TV devices in a future update. The speaker has a dedicated button to disable its camera and microphones, along with an indicator light that activates when images or video are streamed to the cloud.

Echo Time

Echo Time brings Alexa+ to the bedside through a 3.2-inch circular touchscreen with customizable clock faces. Unlike Amazon's camera-equipped speakers and displays, the new clock doesn't include a camera.

Echo Time

Instead, Echo Time uses optional sleep sensing powered by Amazon's Omnisense technology. Amazon says ultrasound can detect breathing patterns and help the clock choose a wake-up time during lighter sleep, within a window of 10 to 60 minutes around a scheduled alarm.

Alexa Photo Frame

Alexa Photo Frame is a separate 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen designed to display pictures from Amazon Photos. Customers can automatically sync selected albums, while Alexa+ can find photos of particular people, pets, or events using natural-language requests.

Alexa Photo Frame

Amazon is also introducing Alexa Home Map, an interactive 3D view of a house and its connected accessories. The interface places lights, locks, cameras, and other devices in their actual locations, allowing customers to control them directly from the map.

Setting up the interior map involves scanning rooms with a compatible iPhone. Amazon plans to introduce the feature in preview later in 2026 through its iOS app and other supported devices.

How Amazon's approach compares with Apple

Amazon's new Echo Show 16 enters a market where Apple is preparing to sell its first dedicated smart-home display. AppleInsider has already compared HomeView with Amazon's Echo Show 8, but the new 16-inch model offers a substantially larger screen with Fire TV built in.

HomeView takes a different approach with a 7-inch display and deeper integration with Apple's existing devices. Siri AI can use personal information from a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, including calendars, messages, and other app content.

Apple says HomeView displays sensitive personal information only after recognizing the user's face and detecting a nearby, recently unlocked iPhone or iPad paired to that person.

The companies also differ in how they handle visual information. Apple says HomeView processes facial and voice recognition inside protected hardware on its A18 chip, while Amazon's Echo Studio uses cloud processing for visual features and provides controls to disable its camera.

Both companies are making conversational AI central to their home products, although some capabilities depend on subscriptions or software updates. Certain Amazon features require Alexa+, which is included with Prime, while Siri AI is available in beta on HomeView and won't reach HomePod mini 2 until a future update.

Pricing and availability

Amazon announced the five devices on October 28, 2026. Four are available now, while the Echo Show 16 is open for preorder.

The Echo Dot costs $99.99, while the Amazon Kids version starts at $109.99. The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available for $249.99, and the standard Echo Studio without a camera remains available for $219.99.

The Echo Time is available for $199.99, with an Amazon Kids version starting at $209.99. The Alexa Photo Frame starts at $199.99 for the black model, while Birch and Walnut wood-frame options cost $229.

items.title: The global memory crisis will annoy everyone until 2030 at least
items.content_html:
The memory crisis isn't going to be solved before 2030, and there's a new shortage brewing that's just going to make things worse and more expensive.

Manufacturers and consumers are already dealing with the effects of high memory demand caused primarily through AI data center and infrastructure buildouts. Now, it seems that the problem will be affecting more components, and for years longer than anyone really expected.

In its Q3 financial results released on Wednesday, memory maker SK Hynix claims it achieved revenues of 104 trillion won ($77 billion) and a net profit of 39.7 trillion won ($29 billion), thanks to record sales.

However, the company is also aware that its high revenue has a backdrop of the memory supply shortage. "AI-driven productivity gains" has helped lead to greater AI adoption, resulting in more investment in infrastructure.

With the prospect of AI data center growth continuing to be steady for the foreseeable future, SK Hynix also points out a supply problem. In its assessment, supplies are not keeping up with the growth of the market.

There's also the technical difficulty of "leading-edge processes" as well as the lengthy construction time to make new manufacturing facilities to consider. SK Hynix expects that demand for memory will continue to exceed supply through 2030.

An expanded problem

While the prospect of waiting years for memory prices to stabilize or even start to return to normal is a bad one, it's not the only issue AI is causing.

According to Nikkei Asia, there's another supply constraint that's affecting electronics producers. Printed circuit boards are in short supply too.

Just like consumer computers and enterprise servers, AI infrastructure relies on printed circuit boards (PCBs) to plug everything into and to get the components working together.

AI server makers have their own custom motherboards, made to be more efficient and to cope with the needs of AI processing. This puts a strain on the PCB market, affecting practically anyone needing a circuit board.

PC manufacturers such as HP and Dell are already locking in with suppliers early, so they can avoid the supply capacity limits that have plagued the memory industry. In turn, this will impact the cost of boards across the industry.

Higher prices, for longer

Once again, this is a big problem for consumers in general, including Apple device users. Like other PC and electronics manufacturers, Apple has to compete in the same market, with very similar constraints.

Apple does have the benefit of its sheer size and the scale of its supply chain operations. It too will use its expertise to secure components long in advance, just as it did to insulate consumers from memory price rises.

However, just like the memory problem, this is something Apple cannot maintain in the long term. Eventually, if prices rise even more, they will be passed down to consumers, increasing the cost of future iPhones and Macs.

It was already expected that the RAM supply crisis would get worse before it gets better. While memory producers fight to build out facilities as fast as they can, it's still a multi-year process that will take a very long time.

Short of a major event cutting AI's appetite for memory and circuit boards, we face quite a few years of painful product pricing.

items.title: How macOS is changing on touchscreens beyond Sidecar, but only a bit
items.content_html:
Apple didn't just put a touchscreen on the MacBook Pro, it made some minor macOS changes to buttons and menus to accommodate your fingers. Here's where they are so far, and what apps will get them first.

The company introduced the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at its "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28. The new models start at $2,899 and $3,399, respectively, with preorders open now and availability beginning November 6.

The laptops run macOS 27 and retain the traditional keyboard and trackpad. Apple has added touchscreen support without replacing the desktop interface that Mac users already know.

One of the clearest changes involves the red, yellow and green buttons at the top-left corner of Mac windows. In its hands-on report, The Verge found that the buttons grow larger when touched, making them easier to select with a finger. A short video posted by Neil Cybart shows the same behavior, although the buttons appear to respond with a slight delay.

A closer look at how window controls in macOS respond to touch. https://t.co/OT8NIiVM4S

— Neil Cybart (@neilcybart) October 28, 2026

The adjustment addresses a practical problem with touchscreen laptops. Controls designed for a precise mouse pointer aren't always large enough to tap comfortably.

Apple's announcement also describes familiar gestures, including swiping to scroll, pinching to zoom and dragging slides between presentations. Users can double-tap a window to fill the screen or flick it into a tiled position.

macOS 27.2 adds more touch-specific controls

Additional interface changes have appeared in macOS 27.2 beta testing, although they haven't all been independently demonstrated on the new MacBook Pro. Some demonstrations use Sidecar, which lets an iPad act as a Mac display.

Apple introduced direct finger control for Sidecar in macOS 27, allowing users to navigate Mac apps on an iPad without an Apple Pencil, as hands-on testing showed in June.

The company's developer guidance confirms that macOS 27 handles Sidecar touch input through gesture recognizers. The capability provides a way to test touch interactions on a Mac without using the new laptop.

In Safari 27.2, tabs lift and enlarge when users drag them to change their order. X user pdfu demonstrated that pressing and holding a tab also opens a touch-specific context menu that omits the usual "Ask Siri" option.

Finder makes a smaller but useful adjustment. Its Edit Tags menu adds more spacing between items when opened with a finger, creating larger targets without permanently changing the menu's compact appearance.

Calendar has another adaptation in macOS 27.2. Events display circular resize handles during touch interaction, giving users a larger area to grab when changing an event's duration.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

None of those adjustments requires macOS to adopt an iPad-style layout. Instead, individual controls respond differently depending on how users interact with them.

The beta findings show that Apple is developing touch-specific interface changes beyond basic gestures. However, they don't confirm which changes will be available on the new MacBook Pro when it ships Nov. 6.

Touch support goes beyond Apple's apps

Apple says many existing Mac apps will support touch immediately because macOS converts finger taps into mouse clicks. The conversion provides basic touch compatibility, but it doesn't make every app's interface easier to navigate with a finger.

Developers can add more advanced touch features using Apple's updated gesture APIs. The APIs let apps recognize finger gestures directly instead of relying entirely on simulated mouse clicks.

Apple's creative software provides examples of what more specialized support looks like. Logic Pro will offer a multitouch software keyboard and on-screen instrument pads, while Final Cut Pro will let editors mark ranges, move clips and pinch to zoom in on a cut.

Pixelmator Pro will also support direct interaction with images, including drawing, painting and selecting content on the display. Apple says the related Creator Studio updates will arrive in November.

Third-party developers are preparing touch features as well. Apple's announcement names Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender and other professional apps, with the listed software updates expected later in 2026.

Apps that accept finger taps won't necessarily offer larger controls or multitouch features designed for the new display.

Apple has also brought Dynamic Island to the MacBook Pro, creating a touch-enabled area for Live Activities, music controls and other information. Users can tap to pause a song or accept an AirDrop request without opening another window.

Spotlight and Siri AI are part of Apple's plans for Dynamic Island, although their availability has conditions. Spotlight moves there only when Siri AI is available and enabled, and Siri AI is currently in beta in macOS 27.2.

Apple has made macOS more touch-friendly without abandoning its familiar desktop layout. It's still unclear how consistently the changes will work across third-party apps when the touchscreen MacBook Pro reaches customers.

A call for attention

Gurman also discussed the OLED XDR displays, including the use of a Dynamic Island, slimmer bodies, and a lighter overall weight. There was even a brief mention of a redesigned hinge so that the screen stays put while users touch it.

items.title: There's a fix if your external SSD won't connect to iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
There are a couple of reasons why your iPhone Duo won't see a connected external drive, but more importantly, there's a solution.

So you have an external drive that plugs into the USB-C port of your old iPhone perfectly fine. But when you connect it to your iPhone Duo, nothing happens.

Not to build up suspense here, there are two possible solutions. One is that if you have the iPhone Duo in a case, take it out and try again.

The other is to change the USB-C cable.

You will typically have had an extension cable when you bought the drive. The odds are that this will do the job, and so would other USB-C cables.

In AppleInsider testing, the problem came up with a Lexar drive that had a USB-C connector built in. The drive came with an extra cable that was intended for camera connections, and that worked.

Why this happens

Clearly if you have a case, it's not surprising if a USB-C connector isn't long enough to reach through to the iPhone. But if the drive did work through the case of that other iPhone, you would expect it to work through a similar case on the iPhone Duo.

Left: the Lexar drive can't be seen when connected directly. Right: use Lexar's provided extension unit for use with cameras and it works perfectly.

The problem is definitely due to the length of the USB-C plug and the depth of the USB-C socket. There's no information from Apple about the iPhone Duo being any different to previous recent iPhones on this issue, but it is.

Equally, there is currently no information from case manufacturers on this point, and there probably won't be. But the extension cable trick will work with any of them.

It's definitely less convenient having to carry an extra cable as well as an external drive. But then the fact that you can do it means you could save a lot of money and buy an iPhone Duo with less storage than you're used to.

items.title: M6 vs M4: How two years and two chip generations change Apple Silicon
items.content_html:
Owners of M4 Macs may feel the temptation to upgrade to the M6 Mac mini, MacBook Pro, or iMac. Here's what to expect with the jump to Apple's newest silicon.

In August 2026, Apple introduced the M6 as its new entry-level chip, as well as the M6 generation itself. Brought out with the Mac mini, the M6 was framed by Apple as a way to benefit more from AI, with changes that made it an ideal chip for machine learning workloads.

The introduction took place just over two years after Apple launched its first M4 chip in the iPad Pro. The M6 is also a two-generation jump for some models, such as the Mac mini, which skipped the base M5 chip completely.

With Apple bringing out more hardware using M6, more consumers are going to look at the new hardware and seriously consider upgrading from their M4 equivalents.

This is the breakdown of what Apple's M6 chip provides, and how it is different from the M4.

M6 vs M4: Specifications
