M6 vs M4: Processes and transistors

The M6 and M4 are made by Apple's usual chip foundry partner, TSMC. However, they are made using two different processes.

The M4 was made using a 3-nanometer process, while the M6 uses a 2-nanometer version.

There are usually quite a few benefits for a so-called die shrink, with the first being density. You can fit more transistors in a smaller process level than a larger one, simply because everything is much smaller.

When it comes to transistors, TSMC was able to squeeze 46 billion onto the M6 die. The M4, meanwhile, has just over half that figure at 28 billion transistors.

M6 vs M4: Die shrinks let you fit transistors more densely.

The more transistors on a chip, the more potential calculations and processes it can perform.

The smaller dies can also get advantages in other areas, such as requiring less power for processing. Heat dissipation is also improved on smaller processes.

The die shrink means that the M6 can run cooler and with less energy than the M4 on comparable workloads.

M6 vs M4: Cores and clock speeds

Modern processors don't just have multiple cores, but multiple core types, too. Cores at different clock speeds can help a system better manage power in relation to performance needs.

A high-performance core may not be used while a system is idling, leaving background work for lower-powered efficiency cores to do. When it comes to completing a task, those performance cores come into play.

The M4 has ten cores in Macs, consisting of four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. A nine-core CPU was also available in the iPad Pro, with three performance cores.

The performance cores are clocked at 4.4GHz, while the efficiency cores run at 2.85GHz.

When it comes to the M6, Apple decided to add a new core type to the equation. Alongside the four performance and six efficiency cores, there were a pair of "super" cores that perform at an even higher level.

In the first M6 release, this meant the super cores ran at 4.79GHz, the performance cores at 4.5GHz, and the efficiency cores at 2.94GHz.

Not only does the M6 run at faster clock rates per-core overall, but there's also the benefit of having two extra cores available.

M6 vs M4: Memory

One of the few advantages the M4 has over the M6 is memory quantity support, at least in theory.

The M4 has been used in devices with configurations between 8GB and 32GB of memory, while the M6 goes from 16GB to 32GB allocations.

The reason for this is that there were iPad Pro models with M4 that had just 8GB of memory. There hasn't been an M6 device with less than 16GB.

M6 vs M4: M6 arrived with the Mac mini. There's not been an M6 iPad Pro yet, at the time of reporting.

That said, the M6 still wins out when it comes to bandwidth.

The M4 has a memory bandwidth maximum of 120GB/s. That's dwarfed by the M6, which goes to 170GB/s.

Memory bandwidth is essential, since Apple relies on using Unified Memory. The same memory is used by the CPU, GPU, and other components to minimize data duplication, which is common when separate pools of memory are being used.

M6 vs M4: Graphics and the Neural Engine

While in previous years, we would separate the GPU and the Neural Engine, changes in Apple's hardware landscape means they should be discussed together.

First, the Neural Engine in the M4 has 16 cores, as is tradition, with the capability of performing up to 38 trillion operations per second.

By comparison, the Neural Engine in the M6 is a "Dual 16-core" version. This means it has 32 cores to play with, double that of the M4.

On the GPU side, the M4 has a few configurations depending on the device, at eight, nine, or ten cores. The GPU also has hardware-accelerated ray-tracing, which helps with rendering graphics.

The M6, meanwhile, has a 12-core GPU in its base configuration. The newer GPUs are always declared as being faster than the previous generations, but the M6 has one more advantage over the M4.

The M6 GPU cores have Neural Accelerators in each core. Introduced with the M5, they handle matrix-multiplication operations, which are a bedrock of processing AI and large language models (LLMs).

While the M6 benefits from double the Neural Engine cores for a start, the GPU's Neural Accelerators gives it a massive advantage when it comes to AI processing in general.

That makes the M6 a quite desirable chip for those working in AI.

M6 vs M4: Benchmarks

A good way to demonstrate the performance difference between the M4 and M6 chips is by benchmarking them on the same sort of hardware. Since the Mac mini exists in both M4 and M6 variants, it's an ideal vehicle for this.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench single-core

Under Geekbench 7's listings, the M4 Mac mini manages a single-core score of 3,277. The super core of the M6 Mac mini helps push it further, right up to 4,002, a 22% improvement.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench multi-core

The multi-core score of the M4 Mac mini is decent, with the ten cores managing 15,304 when working together. However, the faster cores and the increased count in the M6 Mac mini reach 21,881, over 42% better.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench Metal

Under Metal, there's a similar gulf of performance. The M4's 54,227 is heavily beaten by the 89,375 of the M6, a 64% improvement.

M6 vs M4: Two generations of improvement

Looking at the M6 against the M4 was always going to be a performance bloodbath. There is a lot of change that happens between two chip generations, with every small alteration helping to grow the gap.

The M6 certainly is an AI-forward chip, with masses of graphical performance aiding the double-sized Neural Engine. And then there's the CPU core improvements and the additional two Super cores to account for, too.

It's easy to see how much of an improvement the M6 has, which directly translates into everyday tasks. You can certainly see where Apple is going with its future Apple Silicon efforts.

That all said, the M4 is still very capable. It's not what you would consider slow, but the M6 is helping show its age a bit.

items.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion, slashing user options
items.content_html:
DoorDash has announced a deal to buy delivery market competitor Instacart, in a move that will leave users with one fewer iPhone app-based delivery option.

DoorDash announced the move via a press release, noting that the $65-a-share buyout price represents a 26% premium on Instacart's closing price from October 22, 2026. The aggregate transaction consideration will be made up of at least 75% cash, with shareholders able to choose cash or DoorDash shares as payment.

While the deal is yet to be completed, it's in both company's interests for the purchase to go ahead. Termination fees would see Instacart pay $650 million and DoorDash $1.25 billion should the deal falter.

For DoorDash, the deal represents an opportunity for the company to expand beyond restaurant food deliveries and into the grocery market and beyond. Instacart had already held talks with Uber about the potential for a deal that ultimately came to nothing.

Consolidation concerns

While DoorDash believes that the deal to buy Instacart will see consumers "benefit from more choice" and enjoy "affordable delivery and savings," many will have concerns. Consolidation of options within any industry, removing competition, usually means the opposite of what DoorDash claims will happen.

Those who work to deliver food and groceries may also be concerned that their pay will be reduced as a result of the lack of competition in the space. DoorDash again argues the opposite, claiming that there will be more earning opportunities generated by the buyout.

However, while the deal is not expected to be completed until the end of 2027 at the earliest, there are still hurdles to overcome. Regulatory approval is required, and an antitrust review is likely.

Despite that likelihood, the current regulatory situation within the United States is favorable to deals of this kind.

Before the buy, WalMart has command of the grocery delivery market. Should the deal pass, the DoorDash/Instacart combo is estimated to hold around 60%.

items.title: MotionVFX, AI tools feature in Apple Creator Studio's latest update
items.content_html:
Apple Creator Studio has more AI-based updates, with the biggest change being the inclusion of MotionVFX plug-ins and templates.

Apple has been steadily making updates to the Apple Creator Studio, including one in September taking advantage of the new iPhone 18 Pro camera. Its latest update is, however, more AI-focused.

The main change is the inclusion of MotionVFX directly into Final Cut Pro for Mac. The addition brings with it thousands of templates, graphics, titles, and transitions.

There are also tools to help with rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading.

Cross-app workflows have also been improved, with editors now able to open images from their Final Cut Pro timeline directly in Pixelmator Pro without reimporting. There's also advanced image generation, more keyframe easing options, and 23 new transcription languages.

MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro - Image Credit: Apple

Motion also gains its own MotionVFX plug-ins, assisting with color grading and 3D camera tracking. Compressor adds the option to encode Cinematic mode video recorded on an iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo.

As well as working on images from Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro adds Generate Fill, which can edit images based on a user's description. Those generated elements can be inserted as new layers, or merged into existing ones, complete with intelligent masking.

Logic Pro improvements

Logic Pro benefits from a new design that uses Liquid Glass, complete with translucent surfaces.

When it comes to actual features, Logic Pro for Mac gains a new assistant powered by Apple's models as well as those of OpenAI. The assistant can help users navigate workflows, create new songs, set up vocal tracks, or update existing projects.

There's also a redesigned browser that centralizes loops, instruments, and effect patches. An on-device audio analysis tool called "music understanding" can also automatically analyze, classify, and tag sounds added to a user's collection.

The new assistant and design of Logic Pro - Image Credit: Apple

Stem Splitter is being updated with the ability to isolate, replace, or rebalance drum parts, without needing the original multitracks.

A Producer Pack can also be unlocked from the King of Modern Salsa, Sergio George. In the pack, George discusses his signature piano sound, as well as Latin jazz and salsa loops.

Lastly, Voice Memo Sound Studio can reduce room ambience and background noise in recordings from supported iPhone models. Those clips can then be further fine-tuned in Logic Pro.

More AI, more formats

Continuing the AI push, the intelligent assistant based on Apple and OpenAI models is also available in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant can understand document contexts.

In Keynote, it can help design, animate, and refine slides, while in Pages it can draft, restructure, and fine-tune written content. Under Numbers, it can recommend suitable charts and create custom tables using world knowledge.

There's also MCP support, allowing external AI agents and tools to read content, make edits, and perform automations in the iWork package.

Beyond AI, the Content Hub also includes Apple-curated stock video footage, more templates, and themes. Keynote gains support for the Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), and Freeform adds text styles for one-step formatting.

The updates to Apple Creator Studio will be arriving in November, free for existing subscribers.

Apple Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with education customers paying $2.99 per month or $29.99 per year.

items.title: M6 14-inch MacBook Pro vs M5 14-inch MacBook Pro: Baselines compared
items.content_html:
The MacBook Pro line has graduated to M6, with the 14-inch entry-level model getting a timely performance boost. Here's how the new model compares to the previous model.

The M5 14-inch MacBook Pro was introduced in October 2025 as a replacement for the M4 version. It's only been a year, but Apple's done the same thing again, this time to the M6.

The change takes the form of the typical spec-bump update, which is chiefly a performance improvement change rather than one introducing brand new features.

To be frank, with expectations of an OLED variant on the way, there's no real reason to make any changes to the non-OLED model. But, as ever, the chip upgrade warrants a wider look at the new current model and the previous one.

M6 MacBook Pro 14-inch

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip has a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, and Apple's first-ever Dual 16-core Neural Engine.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Design, weight, size

The MacBook Pro has a very well-defined design, namely Apple's aluminum slab aesthetic. It's quite fond of its designs, and doesn't like to change them that much if it can help it.

The M5 MacBook Pro measures 12.31 inches long by 8.71 inches wide, just like the M4 version. Its thickness of 0.61 inches was also identical, and keeps the design fairly thin for a notebook.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Closed, from the front, the M6 is just as thin as the M5 version. - Image Credit: Apple

The only change introduced during the M5 launch was a new Space Black colorway replacing Grey alongside Silver.

As usual for a spec-bump update, the footprint of the M6 version is exactly the same size, as well as thickness.

For weight, there's also no real difference here. The M5 MacBook Pro was 3.4 pounds, which the M6 also matches.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Display

While there is the considerable prospect of an OLED display on the horizon, it is evident that Apple still wants to sell its current MacBook display tech to consumers.

The M5 reused the M4 model's display, meaning it has a 14.2-inch screen with a resolution of 3,024 by 1,964. The pixel density of 254 pixels per inch is typical of Apple's MacBook lineup.

The XDR screen benefited from mini LED backlighting, enabling a million-to-one contrast ratio. Brightness hit 1,000 nits for SDR content, 1,600 nits at a peak for HDR content.

The M5 model also supported a billion colors, Wide Color (P3) gamut, and True Tone. ProMotion enabled refresh rates to adapt, going as high as 120 Hz.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Front view. - Image Credit: Apple

Unsurprisingly, all of this is mirrored in the M6 MacBook Pro, too.

That also includes the dreaded notch, located at the top of the screen and holding a camera. The M5 introduced an optional Nano-texture coating to minimize glare, which the M6 retains.

For external display support, the M5 was able to handle two 6K-resolution 60Hz displays using Thunderbolt. Using the HDMI, you could run an 8K 60Hz display, or a 4K one at 240Hz.

The M6 can do the same thing with external displays.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Performance

The M5 in the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro had ten CPU cores, consisting of four super cores and six efficiency cores. It was joined by a 16-core Neural Engine, a 10-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a Media Engine.

The switch to the M6 brings many performance-related changes. Starting with the CPU, which is a 12-core version, with the usual claims of speed improvements over the previous generation.

The core mix this time is described as two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: The M6 has a performance bump on the M5. - Image Credit: Apple

The Neural Engine is back again, but this time it's a "Dual 16-core" version, meaning it has 32 cores to play with. You can add on top of that the Neural Accelerators in the 12-core GPU, as well as the usual Media Engine for hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding.

Then there's memory bandwidth. For the M5, there was 153GB/s available, but this has been increased to 170GB/s in the M6.

When it comes to performance, Apple claims the M6 model has 1.3 times the render performance in Blender than the M5, 1.2 times faster image processing in Affinity, and 1.3 times faster Xcode code compilation. For the growing AI processing needs of its audience, there's a 1.3 times improvement too.

We can't immediately benchmark the M6 MacBook Pro just yet. However, we can use the M6 Mac mini to give some idea of what to expect in terms of performance gains.

It's not going to be an exact match for the MacBook Pro due to various factors, such as thermal management differences. Even so, it will still provide a ballpark figure.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Single-core benchmarks

For single-core performance in Geekbench 7's listings, the M5 MacBook Pro achieves a pretty good 3,647. The M6 Mac mini, however, does 9.7% better at 4,002.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Multi-core benchmarks

The multi-core benchmark is less tight, with the 17,955 of the M5 beaten by the M6's 21,881. That's a 22% margin that can be partially explained by the extra two cores in the M6.

Lastly, graphics, with the M5 MacBook Pro's score of 72,726 still pretty respectable. However, the 89,375 of the M6 Mac mini is a 23% improvement again.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Metal benchmarks

We know there will be a performance improvement going from the M5 to the M6, as is usual for a new generation. While there's a bit of a jump from each, it's not a bad performance for the M5 at all.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Camera and Audio

The notch of the M5 14-inch MacBook Pro included an improved 12MP Center Stage camera. As the name implied, the camera would reframe the shot so the subject was in the middle, making it extremely handy for video calls.

That 1080p video feed, boosted by an advanced image signal processor, also had Desk View, which faked a top-down view of the desk.

Evidently, Apple decided this worked well enough not to change. It's the same camera in the M6 version.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: The ports, like the rest of the design, are unchanged. - Image Credit: Apple

For audio, the M5 and the M6 both use a high-fidelity six-speaker sound system with force-cancelling woofers. There was also Spatial Audio support for Dolby Atmos content, both through speakers and with AirPods using Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking.

The M5 had a headphone jack capable of working with high-impedance headphones, making it great for audiophiles. This too is maintained for the M6 model.

When it comes to audio recording, the M5 MacBook Pro used an array of three "studio-quality" microphones with a high signal-to-noise ratio and directional beamforming. These persist in the M6 with the same specifications.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Storage, connectivity, power

The M5 MacBook Pro included 512GB of storage at its lowest, with upgrade options for 1TB, 2TB, and 4TB. In March 2026, it cut the 512GB option, leaving the 1TB to 4TB range intact.

For M6, Apple's maintaining this later range, with the lowest capacity at 1TB.

On the physical connectivity side, there are three Thunderbolt 4 ports on both models, along with HDMI and an SDXC memory card slot, as well as the headphone jack. MagSafe 3 is also present for charging duties on both models.

14" MacBook Pro M5

Apple's 2025 14-inch MacBook Pro has an M5 chip and is equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports.

The wireless connectivity on the M5 14-inch MacBook Pro consisted of Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 for accessories. Under the M6, these have been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, though those will only really be beneficial if you have similarly-supportive accessories or wireless network infrastructure.

When it comes to power, the M5 model had a 72.4-watt-hour lithium-polymer battery. Apple claimed it could last for up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web access.

This hasn't changed at all with the M6.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Pricing

The base 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 launched at $1,599, but the global memory crisis had other ideas. The price for the base model rose to $1,999, with the Standard Display, M5 chip, 16GB of unified memory, and 1TB of storage.

Increasing the memory to 24GB cost $200, rising by another $200 for the 32GB maximum. If you wanted more storage, the upgrade to 2TB was $500, while 4TB was another $1,000 on top of that.

The included 70W USB-C adapter could also be upgraded to a 96W version for just $20, while Nano-texture was $150.

The new M6 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 with the Standard Display, 16GB of memory, and 1TB of storage.

The memory upgrade jumps are again $200 to 24GB and $200 more to 32GB. Likewise, going to 2TB of storage is a $500 fee, and 4TB another $1,000 beyond that.

The charger upgrade is once more $20, with Nano-texture a $150 upgrade.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Which to buy?

When it comes to buying a base MacBook Pro from Apple directly, you don't really have much choice in the matter. You're stuck with whatever the newest chip is, which in this case is the M6.

It's also a spec-bump update through and through, with very few internal changes instead of anything major and exterior. That puts the M6 model into the bracket of being aimed at consumers who absolutely need to upgrade, or are buying their first MacBook Pro.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: It's faster and better, but no OLED yet. - Image Credit: Apple

There is no realistic reason to upgrade from the M5 to the M6. Things like the Neural Accelerators helped justify people upgrading to the M5, but this time it's a more muted jump up.

It also doesn't help the M6 that it's in the shadow of a rumored launch of an OLED MacBook Pro. For people wanting a serious upgrade from the M5 MacBook Pro, that is what they will be watching out for, not a small upgrade.

That all said, the M6 has still earned its place as being a pretty good entry-level MacBook Pro, for those who want something a little meatier than a MacBook Air.

Where to buy Apple's M6 14-inch MacBook Pro and M5 14-inch MacBook Pro

Apple's new M6 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 and can be purchased at B&H Photo and Amazon.

The closeout M5 14-inch MacBook Pro, meanwhile, is currently on sale from $1,839 at Amazon. A full rundown of the deals and availability can be found in our M5 14-inch MacBook Pro Price Guide.

items.title: ChatGPT can now manage your iCloud Calendar and iCloud emails
items.content_html:
Thanks to dedicated iCloud plugins, OpenAI's ChatGPT can now use details from your iCloud email inbox to schedule and update events in the Calendar app.

On Tuesday, following the debut of an upgraded M6 iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro, OpenAI revealed that ChatGPT has gained two new iCloud plugins. As a result, OpenAI has greatly improved ChatGPT's compatibility with iCloud email and the Apple Calendar app.

In short, ChatGPT can now read and check your iCloud inbox, create and manage emails, and more. What's even more impressive is that ChatGPT will be capable of updating events on your iCloud calendar, based on the details it can gather from your iCloud emails.

For iPhone, iPad, and Mac users, this will deliver a more personalized experience with OpenAI's virtual assistant. These new iCloud plugins also make ChatGPT more useful on Apple platforms, even beating previous attempts at integrating iOS and ChatGPT.

Well before the arrival of Siri AI, the iOS 18.2 update introduced support for a so-called ChatGPT extension. This let Siri hand off more advanced queries to ChatGPT, with explicit user approval, of course.

This partnership between Apple and OpenAI eventually became the subject of a lawsuit, during which OpenAI later revealed the ChatGPT extension had been "persistently underperforming." It's ultimately no surprise that OpenAI took the exact opposite route, instead giving its chatbot iCloud plugins.

In an X post, OpenAI says its new iCloud Mail and iCloud Calendar plugins for ChatGPT are "available on all ChatGPT plans," implying they won't be available to users without a subscription. This fact alone already puts ChatGPT at a disadvantage, relative to Siri AI on iOS.

Apple's new-and-improved Siri AI, which debuted with iOS 27, already offers system-wide integration. In essence, the virtual assistant already available on newer iPhones by default can manage your iCloud emails and Calendar events without a fee.

Siri AI also supports integration with other built-in iOS and iCloud-compatible apps, including Notes, Contacts, Calendar, and more. While OpenAI's new iCloud plugins are undoubtedly a step in the right direction, ChatGPT will always fall short of what Siri AI can do on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro sales beat iPhone 17 Pro figures, but only because of China
items.content_html:
Contrary to complaints from stock analysts about poor iPhone 18 Pro sales, new supply chain research claims that the demand for the iPhone 18 Pro has been high in China, making up for some weakness elsewhere.

It was already clear that the iPhone 18 Pro had sold well as it appears to have been key to Apple reaching a $5 trillion market valuation. But in a note sent to AppleInsider, Counterpoint Research says that demand has been more patchy and region-specific than with the iPhone 17 Pro.

Sales of the iPhone 18 Pro models in China over the first three weeks after release were up 29% year over year. That was helped, though, by how Apple had more stocks of the new model than they had of the iPhone 17 Pro at launch.

Also, demand for Android smartphones from local Chinese firms fell because of price increases.

This clearly made the iPhone more appealing in China. But the demand in that country was such that the iPhone 18 Pro's overall global sales were up 3.1% compared to the iPhone 17 Pro.

These figures are all for the initial demand of the iPhone models and Counterpoint's associate director Sujeong Lim cautions that "Whether China's outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks."

Lim also says that the research firm is looking to see whether the iPhone Duo's later launch than the other models will cannibalize sales, or generate fresh, incremental demand.

Taking China out of the equation

Counterpoint Research says that in the US, sales were down 4% year over year, and speculates that this is because buyers didn't find sufficient improvements to warrant upgrading for. However, 4% is more likely to be the number of US buyers who elected to wait for the iPhone Duo instead of buying the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Then there was also a dramatic downturn in Japan as sales there were 27% down from the iPhone 17 Pro's figures. However, that was reportedly due in part to increased iPhone prices being exacerbated by higher exchange rates.

As ever, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for the majority of sales across every territory. Although for the 2026 iPhones, 56% were the Max edition, compared to 57% in 2025.

This time Apple split its launch so that it only released the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the new iPhone Duo. The usual base iPhone 18 model will now be launched sometime early in 2027.

One analyst believes this split means Apple has lost sales that it won't get back, which doesn't make sense to us, given the seasonality of the iPhone market. Others have reported that Apple has cut iPhone 18 Pro orders, although JP Morgan analysts have dismissed those claims.

items.title: MacBook Neo 2 now predicted to arrive before summer 2027
items.content_html:
A new report claims that Apple is planning to release a second generation of its hit MacBook Neo in the first half of 2027.

The original MacBook Neo was released in March 2026 and proved to be an enormous success. It was such a hit that there was immediately a belief that a next-generation model would follow, and even unsupported wishful thinking that it would be a touch-screen one.

Now Bloomberg is reporting that the second generation MacBook Neo will launch in the first half of 2027. There are no further details in this report, nor any more precise schedule.

Previously, however, Bloomberg has claimed that the MacBook Neo 2 would be based on an A19 processor and feature 12GB of RAM. The current model uses a A18 Pro processor with 8GB RAM.

Reportedly, the MacBook Neo 2 will also sport a new range of colors. At present, the device is available in Blush, Citrus, Indigo, and Silver.

It can only be speculation, but it wouldn't be surprising if Apple launched the MacBook Neo 2 on the anniversary of the first one in March 2027. Then if there are no further price hikes, the MacBook Neo 2 would probably be priced the same as the current model.

When that was first launched, it cost $599 or $699, mostly depending on storage.. In June 2026, though, Apple raised both tiers by $100, citing the global chip shortage.

items.title: New iMac keeps old design but adds M6 processor
items.content_html:
Apple has launched an updated iMac for the first time since 2024, bringing this longstanding favorite up to the speeds of the latest Mac mini.

If it ain't broke, eventually update it. Apple has released its first update to the all-in-one iMac since the 2024 edition gained an M4 processor.

"iMac is the world's best all-in-one, and today it raises the bar yet again," said Shelly Goldberg, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering in a statement. "With the blazing performance and AI capabilities of M6 supercharging every workflow and the next generation of Apple Intelligence with Siri AI — combined with its stunning 24-inch Retina display, its gorgeous design in seven vibrant colors, and macOS 27 — the new iMac has everything users need to run their businesses, manage their lives, and bring their ideas to life."

Announced ahead of the "Pro and Tell" event that's due to feature the revised MacBook Pro, this iMac release is the next to get a new generation of Apple Silicon. As previously expected, there's been no major redesign to the chassis, which remains as it has been since 2020.

That chassis comes in the same seven colors as the previous edition:

  • Blue
  • Green
  • Pink
  • Yellow
  • Purple
  • Orange
  • Silver

There have been a series of upgrades to the iMac's connectivity, though. It now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, plus Apple says its storage is up to twice as fast as the previous model.

The new iMac with M6 comes in two main configurations:

  • 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, two Thunderbolt ports, from $1,499
  • 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, four Thunderbolt ports, 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, from $1,699

In the former, the 10-core CPU has two super cores, three performance cores, and five efficiency ones. The latter 12-core CPU has two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency ones.

Both versions start with 16GB RAM and 256GB storage. The base 10-core version can be upgraded to 24GB RAM, while the 12-core edition can go to 24GB or 32GB RAM.

That base model can be upgraded to 512GB storage or 1TB. The 12-core version can also go to 2TB storage.

By default, the 10-core edition does not come with Ethernet at all, but it can be configured with 2.5 gigabit Ethernet for $30. The 12-core version has 2.5 gigabit Ethernet as standard.

To upgrade or not

So an outside observer wouldn't notice any difference, but a user would. The jump from M4 to M6 is not as great as when the iMac went from Intel to Apple Silicon, but it is still noticeable.

It's arguable whether it's noticeable enough to be worth upgrading from the M4 edition. But that will become clearer once this iMac can be tested.

Users of the 2023 M3 edition will of course see more of an improvement. But this iMac is really aimed primarily at the remaining Intel Mac users, plus perhaps those on the original M1 Apple Silicon.

Apple says that typical uses such as photo editing are twice as fast as before, though. Overall AI computing speed has doubled, too, because of the dual 16-core Neural Engine, plus higher memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s.

Specifically for AI prompt processing in LM Studio, Apple says that the M6 iMac is five times faster than the previous M4 model. It's up to 12 times faster than the M1 iMac.

The new M6 iMac starts at $1,499. Pre-orders open on October 28, 2026, and it will ship on November 6.
